p: Paul writes 'working together' and never says with whom. The usual reading supplies God.
b: The Greek participle synergountes has no object. Paul has just said that God is making his appeal through the apostles (5:20), the usual reading supplies God, as in 1 Corinthians 3:9, where Paul and Apollos are "God's fellow workers." A few suggest 'with you' (compare 1:24, where Paul and Timothy work with the Corinthians "for your joy") or 'with Christ.' The Plain English Translation leaves the object open, as the Greek does, and the reader will probably supply God, as most do. The choice matters little for the sense: the appeal that follows is God's appeal, delivered by people.

t: Can grace be received for nothing?
p: Paul fears that grace received in Corinth might come to nothing. Churches read that worry differently.
b: The Greek eis kenon means 'to emptiness,' 'with no result.' Paul uses it of his own labor (Galatians 2:2; Philippians 2:16) and, in 1 Corinthians 15:2, 10, 14, of faith or grace that might prove empty. Here the Corinthians have already 'received' grace and are being urged not to waste it. Traditions that teach that a believer can fall away (Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist, Lutheran in its own way) hear a real warning. Traditions that teach that the elect persevere (Reformed, many Baptists) hear a warning that God uses to keep his people, or a test of whether the grace was real. The text itself says only that the danger is real enough to need an appeal.

a: At a time of favor I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you
p: Paul quotes the Servant's promise from Isaiah in its Greek form and says it is happening now.
b: Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 as the Greek Old Testament has it ("I listened to you"). This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "When the time of favor came, I answered you" (Isaiah 49:8), and then, of the "day of salvation," "I helped you." In Isaiah the words are spoken to the Servant, and the context is the return from exile (49:9-13). Paul's own comment, "Look, now," says that the promised day has arrived with Christ and the reconciliation he has just described (5:18-21). Jewish readers have generally taken Isaiah 49 as speaking of Israel and its restoration; Paul does not deny that, but he treats the restoration as begun in Christ, and so as open to the Gentiles who are being reconciled.

a: nobody can point to a blemish on our ministry
p: Paul's 'ministry' is one service; he guards it from the charge that it is flawed.
b: The Greek diakonia ('service, ministry') is the word Paul has used for his whole work (3:7-9; 4:1; 5:18). The verb momaomai comes from momos, a 'blemish,' the word the Greek Old Testament uses of animals unfit for sacrifice (Leviticus 22:20). Paul pictures his service as an offering that must not be marked. Behind this lie the charges he has had to answer: that he is fickle (1:17), that he peddles the word (2:17), that he needs letters of recommendation (3:1). A flawless ministry is Paul's way of saying that what discredits him in Corinth is not his conduct.

a: we show ourselves to be God's servants
p: A word from the letter of recommendation: Paul's proof is his suffering.
b: The verb synistemi means 'to introduce, vouch for, recommend.' Paul used it when the Corinthians asked for letters of recommendation (3:1) and when he denied that he was "commending ourselves again" (5:12). Now he does it, but his credentials are a list of hardships and a list of virtues, which is the opposite of what the 'super-apostles' of 10-13 offer (see 10:12, 18). The word diakonoi ('servants') links the list to the 'service' of 6:3 and to 3:6, "servants of a new covenant."

a: in great endurance, in troubles, in hardships, in distresses
p: Greek and Roman teachers also listed their hardships. Paul's list is built like theirs, with a different aim.
b: Writers of Paul's day, above all Stoic and Cynic philosophers, listed hardships to show that a wise person stays steady. Paul uses the form (here, 11:23-29, 12:10, 1 Corinthians 4:9-13) to a different end: in his own words the hardships do not prove self-mastery but show God's power at work in weakness (4:7-12; 12:9-10). The list here has a clear shape: three general words for pressure (6:4), three kinds of violence (6:5a), three kinds of hardship he chose or accepted (6:5b), then virtues (6:6-7a), then seven contrasts (6:7b-10). Compare Romans 8:35, which uses the same pressure words.

p: Acts records the kinds of trouble Paul lists, some before this letter was written.
b: The Greek akatastasiai means 'disorder, tumults.' Acts shows Paul in a persecution that drove him out of Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:50), stoned at Lystra (Acts 14:19), beaten and jailed at Philippi (Acts 16:22-24) and at the center of the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41). Second Corinthians 11:23-25 adds more beatings, prisons and rod-beatings than Acts tells. The list is not a boast of being tough; it is evidence, for readers who knew some of it, of what the good news had cost him.

p: The Greek word means 'fastings,' and it can mean hunger that was forced on Paul or fasts he chose.
b: Nesteiai is the ordinary word for fasting (Matthew 6:16-18). In a list of hardships it most likely means going without food because there was none, and 11:27 pairs it with "hunger and thirst." Another reading takes Paul to mean chosen fasts, a hardship of devotion rather than of circumstance. The Plain English Translation keeps the wider sense, 'going without food,' so that both readings remain open.

t: Weapons for the right and the left
p: A soldier carried a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left. Paul says righteousness supplies both.
b: The Greek says 'the weapons of righteousness of the right and the left.' A common reading takes the right hand for the sword (attack) and the left for the shield (defense), so that Paul claims weapons for every need. Paul uses armor language elsewhere (Romans 6:13; 13:12; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; Ephesians 6:10-17) and, in 10:3-4, says that his weapons "are not fleshly." The 'righteousness' is probably both God's gift and the right conduct that follows it, as in 5:21.
orig: τῶν ὅπλων τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν (ton hoplon tes dikaiosynes ton dexion kai aristeron)

p: The Greek word means 'deceivers,' and it was used against Jesus as well.
b: Planoi (from the root that gives 'planet,' a wanderer) is 'one who leads astray, a deceiver, an impostor.' Paul has been accused of exactly this (2:17; 4:2; 12:16, where some say he was "crafty" and caught the Corinthians "by deceit"). The Gospel of Matthew uses the same word for Jesus when the chief priests call him "that deceiver" (Matthew 27:63). The seven pairs that follow (6:8b-10) all use the same pattern: how it looks to the world, then how it is. Paul's claim is that the second half is the truth.

a: We are punished, and yet not put to death
p: Paul's phrase seems to echo a psalm of one who was disciplined and not given up to death.
b: The Greek paideuomenoi means 'being disciplined,' a word for training, correction and, here, beating. Psalm 118:18 in Greek says that the Lord "disciplined me severely, but he did not give me over to death." This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "Yah has trained me with hard discipline," and then "but to death he did not give me up" (Psalm 118:18). Psalm 118 was a psalm of thanksgiving sung at Passover, and Paul has already quoted a psalm of the same kind (4:13; Psalm 116:10). The echo is likely rather than certain.

a: Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians
p: Paul almost never uses the name of the people he writes to. He does so here.
b: To 'open the mouth' is a Greek and Hebrew way of saying 'to speak plainly' (compare Matthew 5:2). Paul seldom addresses a church by its people's name: he does so with the Galatians (Galatians 3:1) and the Philippians (Philippians 4:15), and only here with the Corinthians. It shows how personal this appeal is. The wide heart may echo Psalm 119:32, where the Greek says "you made my heart wide" (this site's Plain English Translation: "you open my heart wide").

a: You are not cramped by us. You are cramped in your own feelings.
t: Claude's theory: the narrow and the wide
p: The word for 'cramped' in 6:12 is the same root as 'distresses' in 6:4. Paul may be answering the Corinthians' narrowness with his own.
b: The Greek verb stenochoreo ('to be in a tight space') comes from the same family as stenochoria, 'distress,' in the list at 6:4 (and at 4:8, where Paul is "pressed but not cramped"). The 'wide' of 6:11 (platyno) is its opposite. My suggestion is that the whole passage from 6:4 to 6:13 is built on this contrast: Paul has taken all the narrow places (hardships) and come out wide; the Corinthians have no outward distress and yet are narrow, in their own feelings. I know of no commentary that makes the pun the structure of the passage, though commentators note the verbal link. This is a reading offered for judgment, resting on 4:8, 6:4, 6:11-12.

a: Do not hitch yourselves to unbelievers
p: Verse 7:2 picks up 6:13 as if nothing came between. Four main positions try to explain the gap.
b: Read 6:11-13 and then 7:2, and the thread runs on: 'open your hearts... give us room.' Between them come 6:14-7:1, with a different topic and several words found nowhere else in the New Testament (by this site's word data). Paul wrote it for this letter: the title of Webb's study places it in a 'new covenant and second exodus' setting within the letter; the title of Fee's article says it is about food offered to idols, as in 1 Corinthians 8-10. Paul's own, from another occasion: some say Paul wrote it at another time, for example in an earlier letter, and it was placed here later. Borrowed by Paul: some think Paul took over a Jewish or Jewish-Christian text and adapted it; those who hold this differ on whether he or a later editor put it here. Not Paul's: Betz (1973) asked in the title of his article whether it is an anti-Pauline fragment. The deep dive on this chapter weighs the arguments.

a: a yoke that does not match
t: Mismatched yoke: what it does and does not forbid
p: Found only here. Many think it recalls Torah rules on mixing kinds. Who are the 'unbelievers'?
b: Heterozygountes is built on heterozygos, 'of a different yoke.' The Greek Old Testament uses the adjective in Leviticus 19:19 for breeding two kinds of animals together, and Deuteronomy 22:10 forbids plowing "with an ox and a donkey together" (this site's Plain English Translation). Paul does not quote either law, but he borrows its picture: two creatures of different kinds, pulling one load, will hurt each other. The apistoi ('unbelievers') are the non-Christians of Corinth, mainly pagans. The verse does not say what the 'yoke' is. The Corinthian letters give clues against reading it as a ban on all contact with outsiders: Paul told believers married to unbelievers to stay (1 Corinthians 7:12-14), allowed eating with an unbeliever who invites you (1 Corinthians 10:27), and said he did not mean to cut off dealings with the world (1 Corinthians 5:9-10). What he does forbid is a share in idol worship (1 Corinthians 10:14-22). Churches have applied 6:14 to marriage, to business partnerships and to church life; see the card on this chapter.
orig: ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (heterozygountes), 'being yoked with a different kind'
r: Deuteronomy 22:10; Leviticus 19:19; 1 Corinthians 7:12-16; 1 Corinthians 5:9-10; 1 Corinthians 10:14-22; 1 Corinthians 10:27

t: Beliar: from 'worthless' to a name of Satan
p: A Hebrew word for 'worthless' became a personal name for the chief of evil in the centuries before Paul.
b: Hebrew beliya'al means 'worthless' or 'ruin' and is used of wicked men ("worthless men," Deuteronomy 13:13; 1 Samuel 2:12, this site's Plain English Translation). Here it is Paul's name for Satan (compare 2:11; 11:14; 12:7); see the topic on Satan.

a: the temple of the living God
t: A temple of God among idol temples
p: The Corinthians lived next to temples. Paul tells them that they, together, are God's sanctuary.
b: Greek naos means the sanctuary, the inner house of a god, not the whole temple area (hieron). Paul has already told this church that it is God's sanctuary and that the Spirit lives in it (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; 6:19). 'Idols' (eidola) is Paul's word for the images of pagan worship, as in 1 Corinthians 8:4 and 10:19. Whether Paul wrote 'we are' or 'you are' is treated in the variant on this verse.

a: I will live in them and walk about among them
t: A chain of promises: Leviticus and Ezekiel
p: God's old promise to dwell with Israel, joined from several books, is now said to be true of this mixed church.
b: The words come mainly from the Greek of Leviticus 26:11-12, with Ezekiel 37:27 behind them. This site's Plain English Translation of Leviticus 26:12 reads: "I will walk about among you. I will be your God, and you will be my people." Ezekiel 37:27 reads: "My dwelling place will be with them. I will be their God, and they will be my people." Paul changes 'you' to 'them,' and the Greek en autois can mean 'in them' (each believer) or 'among them' (the community). This is the covenant formula ("I will be your God... you will be my people") that runs from Exodus 29:45 to Jeremiah 31:33 and Revelation 21:3. The paragraph quotes Scripture as a unit: Leviticus and Ezekiel (6:16), Isaiah 52:11 and Ezekiel 20 (6:17), and 2 Samuel 7 (6:18).
r: Leviticus 26:11-12; Ezekiel 37:27; Exodus 29:45; Jeremiah 31:33; Jeremiah 32:38; Revelation 21:3

a: get out from the middle of them
p: Isaiah called the exiles to leave Babylon. Paul calls the church to leave idol worship.
b: The words are from Isaiah 52:11, a call to the exiles to leave Babylon and carry the Lord's temple vessels out clean. This site's Plain English Translation reads: "Get out from the middle of her and keep yourselves pure" (Isaiah 52:11). Paul puts 'them' for 'her.' "I will take you in" echoes the Greek of Ezekiel 20:34, 41 (compare Ezekiel 11:17), where God gathers his people out of the nations. The title of Webb's study places the paragraph in a 'second exodus' (return from exile) setting.
r: Isaiah 52:11; Ezekiel 20:34; Ezekiel 20:41; Ezekiel 11:17; Revelation 18:4; 2 Corinthians 6:2

t: A father to David's son, now to sons and daughters
p: The promise God made about David's son is here said of all believers, and 'daughters' is added.
b: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" is the promise to David's heir in 2 Samuel 7:14 (this site's Plain English Translation). Paul changes 'him' to 'you' (plural) and adds "my daughters," a phrase that may come from Isaiah 43:6 ("Bring my sons from far off, my daughters from the end of the earth"). The early church applied it to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5). Paul's move hands the royal promise to the whole people. Two questions follow. Does this mean the church replaces Israel? Most Christian readers say it enlarges Israel's family. Jewish and 'Paul within Judaism' readers stress that Paul speaks to Gentiles in Christ, and that the words do not take away Israel's own promises. See Romans 9-11.
r: 2 Samuel 7:14; 2 Samuel 7:8; Isaiah 43:6; Hebrews 1:5; Romans 8:14-17; Romans 9:25-26

t: The promises that make holiness possible
p: The promises are the ones just quoted: God living with them, welcoming them and being their Father.
b: 'These promises' are 6:16-18: God's presence, welcome and fatherhood. Paul grounds the command in the gift. The order is the order of the old covenant (Exodus 19:4-6: first "I carried you," then "keep my covenant"). "Flesh and spirit" is not a split of the person into a bad part and a good part: Paul means the whole person, outward conduct and inner life (compare 1 Corinthians 7:34). The Greek hagiosyne ('holiness') is rare, and the verb epiteleo ('carry to the end') is the word used in Philippians 1:6 for God finishing a good work; here believers do the finishing. See the card on Christian perfection in this chapter.
orig: ἐπιτελοῦντες ἁγιωσύνην (epitelountes hagiosynen), 'bringing holiness to completion'

p: Verse 7:2 answers 6:13: 'open your hearts' is now 'give us room.'
b: The Greek choreo means 'make room, hold.' The request echoes 6:11-13 ("open your hearts wide") and joins the chapters. The three denials ("wronged... ruined... taken advantage of") answer the charges that show up in chapters 10-13, where Paul is accused of fraud (12:16-18; compare 2:17; 4:2) and where he turns the charge of corrupting minds back on rival teachers (11:3). The last one, 'taken advantage of' (pleonekteo), is a money word, and it leads into chapters 8-9: Paul will handle the collection in a way that cannot be called 'taking advantage.'
orig: χωρήσατε ἡμᾶς (choresate hemas), 'make room for us'

a: so that we die together and live together
p: A saying of friendship, used also in Greek and Latin writing, for loyalty that goes past death.
b: "To die together and to live together" is a stock expression for faithful friendship in the Greek and Roman world; compare Horace's line "with you I would love to live, with you gladly die" (Odes 3.9.24) and, in the Gospels, Peter's vow to die with Jesus rather than deny him (Mark 14:31). Paul's version is stronger: he and the Corinthians are bound so closely that their fates cannot be pulled apart, in life or death. It also answers the Corinthians' accusation that he is unreliable (1:15-2:4). Compare 4:10-12, where his dying works life in them.

a: I speak to you very frankly
p: Two key words for the Greek city: free speech and boasting. Paul uses both of this church.
b: Parrhesia was the free citizen's right to say everything. Paul claims it toward the Corinthians, as in 3:12 (where he speaks "with great boldness"). Kauchesis ('boasting, pride') belongs to a family of words that appears more often in 2 Corinthians than in any other letter; Paul uses it of what he is proud of in them (7:4, 14; 8:24; 9:2-3) and, in 10:8-13:10, of what he refuses to boast of except in the Lord (10:17). The honor-and-shame setting of Roman Corinth made boasting the way status was won. Paul's own boasting is therefore about others' progress, and he keeps boasting in himself for the 'fool's speech' of chapters 11-12.

p: Paul's story of waiting for Titus, broken off at 2:13, now resumes.
b: At 2:12-13 Paul left the open door at Troas because he did not find Titus there, and crossed to Macedonia. The story stops for four chapters (the 'long digression' of 2:14-7:4) and picks up here, with the same words: no rest, then Titus. In Macedonia are Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, where Paul had planted churches (Acts 16-17); Acts 20:1-2 says that on this journey he spoke much to the believers there and then came to Greece. The "conflicts outside" probably mean opposition to Paul's work there; the "fears inside" are worry about the Corinthian crisis. A few commentators who believe 2 Corinthians joins two letters see the break between 2:13 and 7:5 as evidence; most take it as Paul's way of keeping his readers waiting for the good news.

a: who comforts those who are brought low
t: Comfort: one Greek word, three meanings
p: Paul's word for 'comfort' also means 'urge' and 'encourage'. The letter plays with all three.
b: Parakaleo and its noun paraklesis are 'to call alongside.' They can mean comfort (7:6), urge (6:1; 8:6; 9:5) or encourage, and the family appears nearly thirty times in 2 Corinthians, more than in any other letter (it is packed into 1:3-7). The English must choose: the Plain English Translation uses 'comfort' and 'urge' as the sense requires, and this note keeps the link visible. God "comforts those who are brought low" echoes Isaiah 49:13: "The LORD has comforted his people" (this site's Plain English Translation), and "takes pity on his poor ones." It is the verse next to the one Paul quoted at 6:2.

a: Even if I grieved you by my letter
p: Paul speaks of a letter that hurt. Was it 1 Corinthians, a lost letter, or part of this one?
b: Paul mentions a painful letter at 2:3-4, 9 and here. A lost 'severe letter' written between 1 and 2 Corinthians is one common view: Paul says "I wrote through many tears" (2:4); the letter followed a visit that went badly, and Titus carried it. First Corinthians was the older view. Against it, 1 Corinthians has no clear offense against Paul himself and does not read as written in tears. Chapters 10-13 of this letter are proposed because they are sharper than anything in 1-9; against this, those chapters never mention the offender whom the severe letter was about. If the lost letter existed, nothing of it survives, as with the earlier letter of 1 Corinthians 5:9.

p: Paul uses two Greek words for a change of heart and plays on them.
b: Verse 8 uses metamelomai ('to regret, to feel sorry afterward'), the word used of Judas in Matthew 27:3. Verses 9-10 use metanoia ('repentance,' a change of mind that turns a life around), and the last word of 7:10 is ametameleton, 'without regret.' The sentence is built with care: Paul regretted a moment, but the Corinthians' repentance leads to a salvation no one will regret. The Latin Vulgate renders metanoia with poenitentia ('penance'), which fed the sixteenth-century debate over what repentance is; see the card on 7:10.

t: Godly grief and the grief of the world
p: The difference is not how much one grieves. It is where the grief points.
b: "Grief in God's way" (kata theon) turns toward God and others and ends in repentance and salvation. "The grief of the world" turns in on itself, regret that one was caught or hurt, and ends in death. A reader may set Peter, who "wept bitterly" and was restored (Luke 22:61-62), beside Judas, who "regretted" and died (Matthew 27:3-5), though Paul does not mention either. "Death" here may mean spiritual death, or the literal harm that despair can do. The Plain English Translation keeps the phrase 'in God's way' rather than the older 'godly sorrow' to show that the Greek is about God's direction (kata theon), not about piety.
orig: ἡ κατὰ θεὸν λύπη (he kata theon lype), 'grief according to God'

p: The last item on Paul's list is a word for 'punishment' or 'justice done.' Against whom?
b: Ekdikesis means 'vindication, justice, punishment.' The reading depends on who the wrongdoer was (see 7:12). If it was the man who had wronged Paul, the Corinthians' act was to discipline him; Paul then asks them to forgive him (2:5-11). If it was the man of 1 Corinthians 5:1-5, the 'justice' was the removal Paul had asked for. Either way, the church acted, and Paul now says they have "shown yourselves clean in this matter," which clears them. Churches have drawn on this passage, with 2:5-11, for discipline that aims at repair rather than payback; see the topic on church discipline.

a: the wrongdoer, or because of the one wronged
t: Who did wrong, and who suffered it?
p: Paul names neither man. The identification has changed over the centuries.
b: Three views are held. 1. The wrongdoer is the man of 1 Corinthians 5:1 who lived with his father's wife, and the one who "suffered the wrong" is his father. 2. The wrongdoer is a member who had publicly attacked Paul (perhaps during the 'painful visit' of 2:1) and Paul is the one wronged. 3. The two figures are put in general terms and Paul does not mean particular persons. In every view the point is the same: the letter was not a lawsuit between individuals but a test of whether the church would stand with its founder.

p: A phrase Paul uses of himself in Corinth and of obedient hearers elsewhere. Here it is not terror.
b: "Fear and trembling" appears in Paul at 1 Corinthians 2:3 (his own state when he first came to Corinth), Philippians 2:12 and Ephesians 6:5. It describes respect and a sense of what is at stake, not fright. The Corinthians welcomed Titus with respect because he carried Paul's authority. Obedience (hypakoe) here means answering Paul's letter, and it is the same word Paul uses for what he wants of the church in 2:9 and 10:6. His language of obedience to himself is among the things the 'super-apostles' used against him.
orig: φόβου καὶ τρόμου (phobou kai tromou), 'fear and trembling'

t: 'Grace' is the word for the collection
p: Paul never says 'collection' in chapters 8-9. He uses grace, fellowship, service, blessing and generosity instead.
b: The Greek charis ('grace,' a gift no one earned) appears ten times in chapters 8-9 (8:1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 16, 19; 9:8, 14, 15); eight are the gift for Jerusalem or God's grace in it, and two (8:16; 9:15) are 'thanks'. Paul's other words for it are koinonia ('sharing,' 8:4; 9:13), diakonia ('service,' 8:4; 9:1, 12, 13), leitourgia ('priestly service,' 9:12), eulogia ('blessing,' 9:5), haplotes ('generosity,' 8:2; 9:11, 13) and hadrotes ('abundance,' 8:20). The only plain word for 'collection' is logeia in 1 Corinthians 16:1-2. By never using it, Paul keeps the reader from thinking of a tax or a fund-raising drive; every word he picks makes the gift an act of God's grace passing through the givers. The Plain English Translation says 'grace' for the eight uses that mean grace and 'thanks' where charis means thanks (8:16; 9:15).

p: The Macedonians gave while poor and under pressure. The Greek of 'deep' is 'down to the depth.'
b: Macedonia had been a Roman province since the 140s BC. The churches Paul founded there were at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea (Acts 16-17). The Thessalonians were under attack from their own countrymen from the start (1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14; Acts 17:5-9), and the "great trouble" of 8:2 probably includes that. The Greek kata bathous ('down to the depth') pictures poverty reaching the bottom. Philippi had also sent Paul gifts while he was in Thessalonica (Philippians 4:15-16) and later in Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:9), so these were churches that already knew how to give. Poor people giving is also the point of the Gospel story of the widow's coins (Mark 12:41-44; Luke 21:1-4).
orig: κατὰ βάθους πτωχεία (kata bathous ptocheia), 'poverty down to the depth'
r: Acts 16:11-40; Acts 17:1-15; 1 Thessalonians 1:6; 1 Thessalonians 2:14; Philippians 4:15-16; Mark 12:41-44

t: Who were the 'saints' in Jerusalem, and why were they poor?
p: The gift was for believers in Jerusalem. Scholars give several reasons they needed it, and several reasons Paul cared so much.
b: 'The saints' is Paul's usual name for believers, 'God's holy people'; in Romans 15:26 he names the recipients: "the poor among the saints in Jerusalem" (this site's Plain English Translation). Why were they poor? A famine in Judea (Acts 11:28-30; Josephus, Antiquities 20.2.5 and 20.5.2, Whiston's numbering); the sharing of goods in the early days (Acts 2:44-45; 4:32-35), which may have used up capital; pressure from neighbors; and the plain poverty of a Galilean-and-Judean movement. 'The poor' may also have been a title for the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:10). Why did Paul care? Because the Jerusalem leaders had asked him to "remember the poor" (Galatians 2:10); because Gentiles owed a debt for the spiritual gifts that came from Jerusalem (Romans 15:27); and, in some scholars' readings, because the gift of the nations to Zion fulfilled the prophets (Isaiah 60:5-7). The deep dive on chapter 8 sets out the views.
r: Romans 15:25-28; Acts 11:28-30; Acts 24:17; Galatians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 16:1-4; Isaiah 60:5-7

a: in faith, in speech, in knowledge
t: The gifts Paul praised in 1 Corinthians
p: Faith, speech and knowledge: the first things Paul thanked God for in the first letter, and the things they quarreled over.
b: Paul's thanksgiving in 1 Corinthians 1:5 says the church was "made rich in every way, in all speech and all knowledge." Here the list is nearly the same, with 'faith' and 'eagerness' added. The compliment is also a nudge: the church that excels in speech and knowledge has not yet excelled in giving (compare 1 Corinthians 8:1, "knowledge puffs up, but love builds up"). To "overflow" (perisseuete) in the gift is the test of the rest.

a: He was rich, and yet he became poor for your sake
t: Rich and poor: what did Christ give up?
p: The 'rich' and 'poor' of Christ have been read as his pre-existent glory, his earthly life, or the cross.
b: Pre-existence and incarnation. Many read "he was rich" as Christ's heavenly glory with God and "became poor" as his coming as a human and dying (compare Philippians 2:6-8). Earthly life. Some think the verse need not assume pre-existence and can mean the poverty of Jesus's life and death, which he chose; Paul's own readers would not need more (compare Luke 9:58). The cross. A few stress that his poverty is above all his death. The argument of the passage does not depend on settling this: Paul's point is the pattern of the Giver who gave up for others.

t: Rich in what? A misreading of 8:9
p: Some teachers take this verse to promise money. In context, it is a call to give.
b: Some teachers of 'prosperity' read 8:9 as a promise that Christ became poor so that believers would get rich in money. The context is the reverse. The verse is used to urge poor Macedonians, and Corinthians who were better off, to share with Jerusalem's poor (8:13-15). The riches Paul has in view in this letter are spiritual and shared: the "riches of generosity" (8:2), being "made rich in every way" to give (9:11), the "indescribable gift" (9:15). Paul does not promise believers wealth; he promises that God will supply what they need to go on giving (9:8). Compare Paul's own report in 6:10: "poor, yet we make many rich."
orig: πτωχείᾳ ... πλουτήσητε (ptocheia... ploutesete), 'poverty... might be made rich'

p: 'A year ago' could be only a few months, since new years began at different times.
b: Greek apo perysi means 'since last year.' Ancient years began at different times: the Roman year in January, the Jewish civil year in autumn, and the Macedonian calendar in autumn. Someone who reckoned by one calendar and wrote in another could mean a few months. The usual order is that the plan was begun in 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 and that the Corinthians took the first step soon after, when Titus visited, and then stopped when the quarrel with Paul broke out.

p: The Greek word is the one used of offerings that God accepts.
b: Euprosdektos ('well received, acceptable') is used elsewhere by Paul of the offering of the Gentiles (Romans 15:16) and of his own service in Jerusalem (Romans 15:31), and in 1 Peter 2:5 of the believers' "spiritual sacrifices." The gift is welcome, or rejected, as an offering is. The measure Paul gives is simple: it is judged by what a person has. That is the same rule the Gospels attribute to Jesus when he praised the poor widow (Mark 12:43-44). The word shares its stem with the "time of favor" (euprosdektos, 'acceptable') of Isaiah 49:8 at 6:2. The Plain English Translation says 'favor' there and 'welcome' here, so the link is visible only in the Greek.

p: Paul's word is a fair give-and-take between two groups, not a plan to make everyone equal.
b: Isotes ('equality, fairness') was a Greek ideal of justice. Philo of Alexandria called equality the 'muse' of justice (Who Is the Heir 161, in Yonge's translation). Paul uses the word of a fair balance: at this time Corinth's surplus meets Jerusalem's need, and Jerusalem's own surplus, which Paul may mean as the spiritual gifts of Romans 15:27, meets Corinth's. It also appears in Colossians 4:1, where masters are told to treat their slaves with "justice and fairness." Paul does not ask the Corinthians to give until they are as poor as the saints (8:13); he asks them to share out of what they have (8:12). Compare the first church's practice in Acts 4:34-35.

a: The one who had much had no extra, and the one who had little did not lack
p: Paul quotes the rule of the manna in the wilderness as the pattern for sharing wealth.
b: Paul quotes Exodus 16:18 as the Greek Old Testament has it. This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little did not run short" (Exodus 16:18). The story: God gave each household what it could eat for a day, and nothing could be hoarded (Exodus 16:19-21). Paul uses it for the churches: abundance and need are meant to meet. He does not say that wealth is equalized by miracle, as the manna was; the Corinthians are the ones through whom the balance is made. Rabbinic tradition linked manna with trust in God day by day: whoever has bread in the basket and asks what he will eat tomorrow is of little faith (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 48b).

t: Claude's theory: surplus that does not rot
p: In the manna story, what was stored beyond need went bad. Paul may be picturing Corinth's surplus the same way.
b: In Exodus 16:20 anyone who kept manna over until morning found it full of worms. Paul does not mention this, only the first half of the story (16:18). I suggest, as my own reading, that the unspoken second half sharpens his point: wealth kept beyond need is like manna kept overnight, and the collection is the way the Corinthians' surplus is put to use before it spoils. This is my own reading, not one I found in a commentary. It rests on 8:13-15 and Exodus 16:18-21 and is offered only as a reading to test.

a: the brother whose praise in the good news is told in all the churches
p: Paul names neither of the two brothers sent with Titus. Guesses go back to the early church.
b: Paul calls him only "the brother." Luke is one candidate: Jerome, in Lives of Illustrious Men 7, names Luke's Gospel as the one Paul means by "praise in the good news" and states the identification without doubt. Acts 20:4 also lists delegates from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe and Asia traveling with Paul; the brother of 8:18 might be one of them, or a Macedonian whose name Paul left out. The second brother, "tested in many things," is equally unnamed (8:22).

p: The delegate who handled the money was picked by the churches, not by Paul.
b: The Greek cheirotoneo originally meant 'to vote by raising hands.' It later came to mean 'to appoint, ordain': the Didache tells churches to "appoint for yourselves bishops and deacons" with the same verb (Didache 15:1). Here the sense is still the earlier one: the churches themselves chose a representative to travel with Paul and Titus. This was a safeguard (8:20-21): in a world where moving money drew suspicion, Paul made sure the delegates were chosen and the accounts were not his alone. His plan, in effect, was to have the money carried by a committee, not by one person.

a: not only before the Lord but also before people
p: Paul takes a line from Proverbs about being good in God's sight and people's sight, and uses it for handling money.
b: The wording matches the Greek of Proverbs 3:4 ("plan ahead for good things before the Lord and before people"), which Paul also echoes in Romans 12:17. The Hebrew of Proverbs 3:4 speaks of finding "favor and good insight in the eyes of God and man"; the Greek translator turned that into a call to plan ahead for what is honorable. Paul's practice here is early church accountability: the collection is handled by named delegates chosen by the churches, so that no one "could blame us" (8:20).

p: The Greek is apostoloi. Here it means 'envoys,' not the office held by the Twelve and by Paul.
b: Apostolos comes from apostello, 'to send.' For Paul it names the office of those sent by Christ himself (Galatians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 15:7-9), but the word also means any envoy sent on an errand. Epaphroditus is the "apostle" (messenger) of the Philippians (Philippians 2:25), and the two brothers here are "apostles of the churches." The Plain English Translation follows the project's rule: 'apostle' for the office, 'messenger' for a general envoy. Paul's critics in chapters 10-13 claim a higher kind of apostleship, which is one reason he is careful to say which sense he means.

t: Achaia, Macedonia and the contest of giving
p: Paul told each province about the other. The Macedonians were the example for Achaia, and Achaia was first the example for them.
b: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital (Acts 18:12 names its governor, Gallio). Paul played the two provinces against each other, gently: in chapter 8 the Macedonians are the model; here Achaia's readiness had spurred the Macedonians (9:2). This was the honor-driven world of Greek and Roman cities, in which public giving (euergetism) won status. Paul uses the habit but changes its aim: the gifts do not honor the givers; they bring "thanks to God" (9:11-12).

a: as a blessing and not as greed
p: Two Greek words, eulogia and pleonexia. Whose greed does Paul mean?
b: Eulogia ('blessing') can mean a generous gift (as in Genesis 33:11 and 2 Kings 5:15, where the Hebrew 'blessing' is a present). Pleonexia ('wanting more') means grasping. Three readings: (1) a gift given in generosity, as opposed to one squeezed out of reluctant givers (the plainest sense); (2) a gift that blesses the receivers rather than a grab by Paul, who has been accused of taking advantage (7:2; 12:16-18); (3) a contrast between a blessing for the Corinthians and the greed of withholding. All three agree that the gift must be willing. Paul's rule in 9:7 follows from it.

p: A farmer's rule, found in Proverbs and echoed across the New Testament, is applied to giving.
b: "Sows with blessings" is the Greek ep' eulogiais, 'on the basis of blessings,' meaning generously. The picture of reaping what is sown appears in Proverbs 11:24-25 (this site's Plain English Translation: "Someone scatters freely, and he ends up with still more"), in Hosea 10:12 ("Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap by the measure of loyal love"), and in Galatians 6:7-9 and Luke 6:38. Paul's version is about giving and the harvest God gives back. What God gives back is told in 9:8-11: sufficiency to give again, a larger harvest of "righteousness," and thanks to God.

p: Teachers of 'seed-faith' read 9:6-10 as a promise of money in return. Most others do not.
b: Teachers of the prosperity gospel and 'seed-faith' take 9:6-10 as a promise that gifts to a ministry will return in money. A common reply is that Paul's harvest is "the fruits of your righteousness" (9:10), thanksgiving and prayer from the poor (9:11-14), and God's supply of what is needed so that giving can go on (9:8). The occasion is a gift to poor believers, not a payment to an apostle (Paul refuses support from Corinth in 11:7-9). Wesley's rule is often quoted for the alternative: 'gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can' (The Use of Money, sermon 50).

a: For God loves a glad giver
t: A line from the Greek Proverbs
p: Paul's words seem to come from a verse found in the Greek Old Testament but not in the Hebrew.
b: "God loves a cheerful giver" matches the Greek text of Proverbs 22:8a ("God blesses a cheerful and generous man"). That line is in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew text, so this site's Plain English Translation of Proverbs 22:8 does not have it. Paul has "loves" for the Greek's "blesses." The Greek word for 'cheerful,' hilaros, is the root of the English word 'hilarious,' and means joyful and without reluctance. Paul does not here say how much to give. He gives the manner (decided in the heart, not from sorrow or force) and the reason (God's love). See the card on giving and tithing.

p: The Greek word is one the Stoics prized. Paul's version depends on God.
b: Autarkeia ('self-sufficiency') was the Stoic ideal of a person who needs nothing from outside. Paul takes the word and sets it in God's hand: believers have "all you need," not to keep, but to "have plenty for every good work." In Philippians 4:11-13 he calls himself autarkes ('content') in want or plenty because of Christ, and in 1 Timothy 6:6 "godliness with contentment" is great gain. The 'enough' is for giving as much as living.

a: He has scattered abroad. He has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.
p: A psalm about the person who fears God. In Jewish speech, 'righteousness' came to mean giving to the poor.
b: The quotation is Psalm 112:9 in the Greek form. This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "He has scattered, he has given to the needy. His righteousness stands for all time." The 'he' of the psalm is the person who fears the Lord (112:1); Paul uses it of the generous believer, and in 9:10 may shift to God, who supplies the seed. In Hebrew, tsedaqah ('righteousness') came to mean giving to the poor, as it still does in Judaism today (tzedakah); the Mishnah lists kind deeds among things with "no fixed measure" (Mishnah Peah 1:1). Paul's 'righteousness' here probably carries the Jewish sense of generosity as well as God's gift of right standing (5:21). The two meet in 9:10: the harvest of your righteousness.

a: The One who provides seed for the sower and bread for food
p: God, the giver of seed and bread, is the one who multiplies the Corinthians' harvest.
b: Paul's words follow Isaiah 55:10 (Greek), where God sends rain so that the earth gives "seed to the one who sows and bread to the one who eats" (this site's Plain English Translation). In Isaiah the point is that God's word does what he sends it to do. Paul applies it to giving: the God who feeds the world feeds the giver. "The fruits of your righteousness" may echo Hosea 10:12, "Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap by the measure of loyal love." With 9:9, righteousness here means generosity. The King James Version, following the Textus Receptus, reads verse 10 as a wish ("may he supply"); the earlier manuscripts have a promise ("he will supply"); see the variant.

p: Two words in a row: diakonia (service) and leitourgia (priestly service).
b: Paul writes "the service (diakonia) of this leitourgia." Leitourgia is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the priests' and Levites' work in the sanctuary, and the root of English 'liturgy.' In Romans 15:16 Paul calls himself a leitourgos (a priestly minister) offering the Gentiles to God, and in 15:27 says the Gentiles owe it to Jerusalem to "serve" them in material things with the same verb. Calling the collection a leitourgia gives it the dignity of worship. In ordinary Greek, though, the word also meant a public service paid for by a rich citizen, so Paul's readers heard both a temple word and a civic one.

a: your obedience, which goes with your confession of the good news of Christ
p: Giving is called obedience to the good news. The saints in Jerusalem will see it and praise God.
b: The Greek says "the submission (hypotage) of your confession to the good news." Faith that confesses must also act. The recipients, the Jewish believers of Jerusalem, will see that Gentile faith is real when it shows itself in a gift to Jews. This is one reason Paul worried whether the gift would be "acceptable to the saints" (Romans 15:31): the collection was a test of the unity of Jews and Gentiles in one church.
orig: ὑποταγῇ τῆς ὁμολογίας (hypotage tes homologias), 'submission of confession'

a: his gift that is beyond telling
p: Paul ends the two chapters with thanks for a gift. Which gift?
b: Readers have proposed several answers. Christ himself, whose self-giving began this appeal (8:9). God's grace in the Corinthians' own giving (9:14). The whole of salvation, including the unity of Jews and Gentiles that the collection shows. Others think of the Spirit. The Greek anekdiegetos ('unable to be told') occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. One way to hold these together is to read all of them at once: the gift of Christ, which sets every other gift going. The Plain English Translation keeps the word 'gift' without a capital and lets 8:9 and 9:14 show what is meant.
